1.title: Electrical Energy, Resistance, and Power
1.text:
Electrical Energy, Resistance, and Power

Circuits transform electrical energy into useful forms like light and motion, with some always becoming thermal energy.

Our big question for this lesson: how do we use electrical energy? Energy supplied to a circuit can be transformed in lots of useful ways. A lamp, for instance, turns electrical energy into radiant energy, light. Picture the image of Earth at night from the start of this module: all those glowing cities are circuits transforming electrical energy into light.

But not all the energy delivered to a lamp ends up as light. Lightbulbs, especially incandescent ones, get hot. Some of the electrical energy becomes thermal energy.

2.title: Heating a Resistor
2.text:
Heating a Resistor

Current through a resistor raises its thermal energy as moving electrons collide with the resistor's atoms.

Why does a resistor heat up? As current flows, the moving electrons bump into the resistor's atoms. Those collisions make the atoms jiggle faster, and faster-moving atoms mean a higher temperature.

Space heaters, hot plates, and the heating element in a hair dryer are all designed to turn electrical energy into thermal energy. These appliances, like the ones in Figure 14, act like resistors in a circuit. That's why they heat up when you switch them on: current flows through their resistive elements, and the electron collisions turn electrical energy into thermal energy.

4.title: Power in a Resistor
4.text:
Power in a Resistor

Power in a resistor is P equals the square of I times R, or P equals the square of delta V divided by R.

When charge q moves through a resistor, its potential drops by delta V, so its energy drops by q times delta V. What usually matters most, though, is the rate of energy change: the power, P equals E over t. We know current is I equals q over t, and power is P equals I times delta V.

For a resistor, delta V equals I times R. Substitute that into P equals I delta V, and you get P equals the square of I times R. So the power in a resistor is proportional to the square of the current and to the resistance.

If you know delta V and R but not I, substitute I equals delta V over R instead. Then P equals the square of delta V, divided by R.

5.title: Power and Thermal Energy
5.text:
Power and Thermal Energy

Thermal energy from a resistor is E equals P t, which equals the square of I times R times t, or the square of delta V times t divided by R.

Power is the rate energy changes form. In a resistor, electrical energy becomes thermal energy, and the resistor's temperature rises. The resistors in an immersion heater do this fast enough to bring water to a boil in a few minutes.

If the power stays steady, then after a time t, the energy turned into thermal energy is E equals P times t. Using our two power equations, that's also E equals the square of I, times R, times t. Or E equals the square of delta V, times t, divided by R.

6.title: Superconductors
6.text:
Superconductors

A superconductor is a material with zero resistance.

A superconductor is a material with zero resistance. Nothing holds back the current, so there's no potential difference across a superconducting wire. Since the rate of energy transformation is I times delta V, and delta V is zero, a superconductor carries current without turning any energy into thermal energy.

The catch? Today, almost all superconductors must be kept colder than about 100 kelvins. Right now they're used in things like MRI magnets. Someday, superconducting cables might carry electrical power efficiently to cities from faraway power plants.

7.title: Example Problem 3, Electric Heat
7.text:
Example Problem 3, Electric Heat

P equals the square of delta V divided by R, and E equals P t.

A heater has a resistance of 10.0 ohms and runs on 120.0 volts. What's its power? And how much thermal energy does it supply in 10.0 seconds?

Step one: analyze and sketch. Sketch a 120.0-volt source connected to a 10.0-ohm resistor. Known: R is 10.0 ohms, delta V is 120.0 volts, and t is 10.0 seconds. Unknown: P and E.

Step two: solve. Since we know R and delta V, use P equals the square of delta V over R. The square of 120.0 volts, divided by 10.0 ohms, is 1440 watts, or 1.44 kilowatts. Then E equals P times t: 1.44 kilowatts times 10.0 seconds is 14.4 kilojoules.

Step three: evaluate. Power is in watts and energy in joules. For the size: ten to the second, times ten to the second, times ten to the negative first is ten to the third, so kilowatts makes sense. And ten to the third times ten to the first is ten to the fourth, so about 10,000 joules makes sense too.

8.title: Providing Electrical Energy
8.text:
Providing Electrical Energy

Joule heating loss, or the I-squared-R loss, is the unwanted thermal energy produced in wires.

How can energy from a hydroelectric dam, like the one in Figure 15 on the Columbia River, travel long distances with as little turned into thermal energy as possible? Wires transform energy at the rate P equals the square of I times R. Engineers call that unwanted thermal energy the Joule heating loss, or the I-squared-R loss.

Every wire has some resistance, which depends on its length. The thick wire carrying current into a home has about 0.20 ohms per kilometer. For a house 3.5 kilometers from the power plant, the wire goes there and back, so R is 2 times 3.5 kilometers times 0.20 ohms per kilometer, or 1.4 ohms.

An electric stove might draw 41 amperes. The power lost in the wires is the square of 41 amperes, times 1.4 ohms, which is about 2400 watts. All of that becomes thermal energy and is wasted!

9.title: Electric Transmission Lines
9.text:
Electric Transmission Lines

Transmitting power at high voltage keeps the current low, which cuts the I-squared-R loss.

To cut the waste, we could lower the current or the resistance. Low-resistance cables, made thick from highly conductive metal, are expensive and heavy. And since the loss depends on the square of the current, lowering the current pays off much more.

Power delivered is P equals I times delta V. So if we raise the voltage, we can deliver the same power with less current. That's why long-distance transmission lines run at voltages far above household voltage, some at more than 500,000 volts. The low current keeps the I-squared factor small.

Before the energy reaches you, substations step the voltage down, for example to 2400 volts, and then again to 240 or 120 volts for use in homes.

10.title: The Kilowatt-Hour
10.text:
The Kilowatt-Hour

A kilowatt-hour is 1000 watts delivered for 1 hour, equal to 3.6 times ten to the sixth joules.

Power is the rate energy is delivered, but on your electric bill, like the one in Figure 16, you pay for energy, not power. The energy a device uses is its power in joules per second, or watts, times the number of seconds it runs. Joules per second times seconds gives joules.

A joule, also called a watt-second, is far too small for selling electricity. So electric companies use a bigger unit, the kilowatt-hour. One kilowatt-hour is 1000 watts delivered continuously for 3600 seconds, 1 hour, which is 3.6 times ten to the sixth joules. Smart meters track how many kilowatt-hours you use.

Not many household devices need more than 1000 watts. The big ones are water heaters, stoves, clothes dryers, microwave ovens, space heaters, and hair dryers.
